Dimanche 23 mars, les élections fédérale: On Sunday, March 23, the federal election was called. The various political parties are starting to tour the country to present their platforms.
Pour comprendre comment se sentent les j: To understand how young people are feeling and how they see this election, the La Converse team asked university and CEGEP students about their concerns. Many spoke of fears about economic and political relations with the United States, the rising cost of living, and the possibility of new immigration measures. Talking with these young people last Monday, I sensed a desire to get involved and to question the current political situation, but I also sensed that some didn’t know how to go about it.
J’ai fait des recherches sur la particip: I did some research on citizen political participation over the past few years, and I noticed that turnout among 18- to 24-year-olds has been declining since the 2015 election. That raised several questions for me: Why does young people’s interest erode a little more with each new election? How could the various political parties encourage young adults to get involved? Why are the current elections particularly important for young people?
Je suis ensuite retournée questionner de: I then went back to question young voters, those who will go to the polls for the first time on April 28. They all seemed interested in their own way. All of them want to vote, even if they admit they haven’t looked into all the issues at stake in depth.
<strong>Un cercle vicieux semble de plus: A vicious circle seems to be taking shape in the relationship between politicians and young people. Political parties are addressing young people less and less in their platforms or on their communication channels. Young people, in turn, reportedly feel less and less represented by these institutions and gradually lose the desire to stay informed and get involved. For less than 10 years now, this circle has been tightening, and young people are tending to stay away from the polls.
Guerre commerciale, tarifs douaniers, en: Trade war, tariffs, the environment, immigration and the cost of living: these topics are on the lips of every young voter. Many wonder how to navigate this ocean of complex concepts while trying, as best they can, to identify with the parties in the race.
Je me suis rendue dans la cafétéria du c: I went to the cafeteria at Cégep Marie-Victorin to talk to a few students. The space is roomy and bright, ideal for conversation. Young people aged 18 and 19 share their concerns, talk about how they’re getting informed during this campaign, and put forward solutions.
Avril, 18 ans, constate que son entourag: Avril, 18, notes that the people around her are talking more and more about current political issues. She explains: “I find that our generation, Generation Z, is more involved. We’re also more opinionated than previous generations.”
Une distance ressentie entre l’univers p: A felt distance between the political world and young people’s realities comes through in many of the accounts. “I feel like no one ever speaks to us directly. We see all kinds of news on TV, but nobody tells us, ‘Young people, we have solutions for you!’ Maybe if they spoke to us directly, we’d listen more,” says Maïka, 18.
Pour plusieurs, les réseaux sociaux sont: For many, social media is the future of communication between the political world and young voters. They all follow political parties’ news more on TikTok or Instagram. “It would even be good to have more explainers on social media. A lot of people haven’t taken a politics class and don’t necessarily understand what’s going on right now,” explains Ariana, 18.
« J’ai l’impression que ce qui circule d: “I feel like what’s already out there on social media is kind of forced. The message gets across, but I don’t sense any real interest from the parties in reaching us,” adds Gabriel, 18.
Ces jeunes ont tous l’intention de voter: These young people all intend to vote. It will be a first for them. There is a real desire to learn about political news and to engage with the issues that affect them most, even though they don’t feel directly spoken to by the parties.
Au cours des trois dernières élections f: Over the last three Canadian federal elections, turnout among 18- to 24-year-olds has only gone down. According to Elections Canada data, it was nearly 57% in 2015, then about 54% in 2019, before dropping to 46.7% in the most recent election, in 2021. That’s 10 percentage points lower in just a few years.
À ce moment, on constate que la particip: At this point, we see that electoral participation rises with age. The turnout gap is quite striking. While nearly 47% of 18- to 24-year-olds vote, nearly 75% of 65- to 74-year-olds cast a ballot. This trend is the same across the country.
Ces données montrent que les citoyens le: This data shows that older citizens carry more electoral weight. But why do young people keep losing a little more interest with each election?
<strong>Entre milieu communautaire et di: Between the community sector and political discourse
Pour essayer de comprendre le phénomène,: To try to understand the phenomenon, we made our first stop at the Centre lasallien Saint-Michel to talk with Stéphanie Germain. The executive director of Éduconnexion and community organizer works at the heart of Montréal communities. She works with high school students and young adults in several neighbourhoods across the city. Stéphanie knows how important the current election is for young people.
« Si je me fie à ce que j’entends des je: “Based on what I hear from the young people I work with, there’s a certain feeling of being erased. Young people don’t feel considered by politics, but that doesn’t mean they’re not getting involved,” she explains.
L’écart entre les réalités des jeunes él: The gap between young voters’ realities and the various parties’ platforms is widening, according to the community organizer. “Elections happen every four years, so for me, we can’t expect young people to be mobilized at that specific moment,” she points out. “Politicians come to our offices to talk with young people only a month or two before the election starts. We should be consulting them all year long.”
Au cours de la première semaine de la ca: During the first week of the election campaign, Stéphanie felt a tension, a buzz in her community. The current state of economic and political relations with the United States is raising questions. “I thought to myself: ‘If we, as adults, are feeling anxious about all this, what must young people be going through?’ Knowing that politicians often speak a language that is completely disconnected from their realities,” Stéphanie observes.
Avec Éduconnexion, elle veut offrir un e: With Éduconnexion, she wants to offer a space for discussion on current political questions and issues. The organization focuses on civic engagement and participation. “Creating spaces of expression for young people is a priority!” she says. By organizing evenings called “Jeunesse en conversation,” Stéphanie is trying to break this vicious circle of misinformation and lack of political involvement. The goal is to give voters and future voters some grounding. Every Friday evening, young people aged 14 to 19 come together to talk among themselves and with specialists from various fields. The evenings are themed around civic engagement, but also cover varied topics such as geopolitics, art, the environment and global citizenship education. A special evening is planned for the election.
« On est dans une période anxiogène, et: “We’re in an anxiety-inducing period, and I find there aren’t enough spaces to take the time to debate current events, what’s being heard in the media, and even to talk about how young people are feeling, what worries them,” Stéphanie concludes.
<strong>La politique provinciale plus in: Provincial politics more interesting to young people
Prochaine étape, André Lamoureux vient p: Next, André Lamoureux comes by our offices for a coffee. He is a specialist in Quebec and Canadian politics and a professor in the Department of Political Science at the Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM). According to him, young people’s participation in the electoral process has historically come in waves. “For the average person, the federal level is a bit more abstract. At the provincial level, as we know, it’s about culture or education. Young people mobilize more because those are issues that affect them in a more concrete way.”
Il souligne la forte incidence des décis: He stresses how strongly the Canadian government’s decisions affect citizens’ daily lives: “There are many areas of jurisdiction that fall under the federal government and, whatever one may think, it has an effect on our lives every day, especially right now with Donald Trump’s offensive. The federal sphere of intervention is very important.”
L’engagement citoyen de la jeunesse n’es: He believes young people’s civic engagement isn’t sought out enough. In his view, the education system should teach more about how political life works, to better prepare 18- to 24-year-olds outside of election periods.
Un autre manquement important concerne l: Another significant shortcoming concerns the involvement of the political parties themselves. “Getting young people involved starts with the party’s platform. Parties need to take positions that speak to young people. From there, we can organize gatherings to advance those causes with them, by supporting them,” explains Mr. Lamoureux.
Selon le spécialiste, comme les jeunes s: According to the specialist, because young people go to the polls less and less, parties are less and less inclined to reach out to them. It’s a kind of vicious circle taking hold. “These are ways of working that take time to establish within parties. It doesn’t happen overnight. It has to be part of a permanent trajectory,” he says.
